sections.name: Perception
tips: Exam-style questions from Phineas's kit for this deck. Read every choice before you pick: the wrong ones are common mix-ups.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes selective attention?
options: Focusing conscious awareness on one particular stimulus and not something else
Noticing every stimulus in the environment equally
The weakest stimulus a person can detect
Using past experience to interpret what you sense
questions.exp: Selective attention = focusing on one thing and NOT something else.

questions.stem: In a class demo, the word GREEN is printed in purple ink, and students must say the ink color. Many answer slowly or say "green" by mistake. This demonstrates:
options: The Stroop effect
Change blindness
The cocktail party effect
Weber's law
questions.exp: The Stroop effect is the delayed reaction when you must say the color of a word instead of the word itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of change blindness?
options: Between shots in a movie, an actor's drink switches from full to empty, and most viewers don't notice.
A driver talking on the phone doesn't see a pedestrian in the crosswalk.
At a noisy party, you hear your name from across the room.
You can hear a watch ticking 20 feet away.
questions.exp: Missing a CHANGE = change blindness. Not seeing the pedestrian at all is inattentional blindness, the trap answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of inattentional blindness?
options: While focused on texting, Ben walks past a bright yellow car parked right in front of him and never sees it.
An actor's shirt changes color between scenes, and viewers miss it.
You notice one red dot in a field of blue dots.
Your music goes from volume 5 to 10, and you notice.
questions.exp: Failing to see a visible object because attention is elsewhere = inattentional blindness. The shirt is change blindness.

questions.stem: What do change blindness and inattentional blindness have in common?
options: Both happen because attention is directed elsewhere.
Both are caused by damage to the occipital lobe.
Both involve hearing rather than vision.
Both are forms of extrasensory perception.
questions.exp: Both come from attention being directed elsewhere. The difference is missing a change vs. missing an object.

questions.stem: A student is so focused on her notes in a noisy cafeteria that she doesn't notice her friend sit down right across from her. Which concept best explains this?
options: Inattentional blindness
The cocktail party effect
The absolute threshold
Precognition
questions.exp: Her friend was fully visible, but her attention was directed elsewhere.

questions.stem: At a crowded school dance, Lena can focus on her friend's voice and tune out everyone else. This best illustrates:
options: The cocktail party effect
The pop-out phenomenon
Change blindness
The difference threshold
questions.exp: Focusing auditory attention on one voice while filtering out others is the cocktail party effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why you might suddenly notice your own name being said across a noisy cafeteria?
options: Your brain can register your name even amongst background noise.
Your absolute threshold for sound drops in loud places.
Top-down processing shuts off in noisy places.
Change blindness makes you notice sounds.
questions.exp: That's part of the cocktail party effect on your slides.

questions.stem: In a crowd of people wearing black, one person in a bright orange jacket instantly catches your eye. This is:
options: The pop-out phenomenon
Inattentional blindness
The Stroop effect
Clairvoyance
questions.exp: Something different popping out to get your attention is the pop-out phenomenon.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the difference between bottom-up and top-down processing?
options: Bottom-up starts with sensory receptors sending information up to the brain (sensation); top-down uses knowledge, experience, and context to interpret it (perception).
Bottom-up uses past experience; top-down uses only the senses.
Bottom-up happens only in vision; top-down only in hearing.
They are two names for the same process.
questions.exp: Bottom-up = sensation. Top-down = perception.

questions.stem: Looking at a messy handwritten note, you see a squiggle and recognize it as the number 15. Recognizing what the squiggle means is an example of:
options: Top-down processing
Bottom-up processing
The absolute threshold
Selective attention
questions.exp: Your slides: being aware of the squiggle is bottom-up; knowing what it means is top-down.

questions.stem: You can read a paragraph where the middle letters of every word are scrambled, as long as the first and last letters are in place. Which of the following best explains this?
options: Top-down processing: the mind reads each word as a whole
Bottom-up processing: the eyes read every letter separately
The Stroop effect
Weber's law
questions.exp: The mind doesn't read every letter by itself, but the word as a whole. That's top-down.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of bottom-up processing?
options: Receptors in your skin register the cold of an ice cube and send that information up to the brain
Recognizing a friend's messy handwriting because you've seen it before
Reading scrambled words because you know the language
Using the context of a sentence to figure out a smudged word
questions.exp: Bottom-up = receptors registering information and sending it up. The others all use knowledge or context (top-down).

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the absolute threshold?
options: The weakest amount of a stimulus a person can detect 50% of the time
The smallest change in a stimulus a person can notice 50% of the time
The point at which a stimulus becomes painful
The constant amount a stimulus must change to be noticed
questions.exp: Absolute = detecting it at all. The second option is the difference threshold, the trap answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of an absolute threshold?
options: Hearing a watch ticking 20 feet away
Noticing your music went from volume 5 to 10
Noticing 1 ounce added to a 10-ounce weight
Not noticing an actor's shirt change color
questions.exp: The watch is the faintest sound you can detect. The other two "noticing" options are about changes (difference threshold).

questions.stem: The difference threshold (just noticeable difference) is best described as:
options: The minimum amount something needs to change before a person notices the change 50% of the time
The weakest stimulus a person can detect at all
The ability to focus on one voice in a crowd
Perceiving events you didn't witness
questions.exp: JND = the smallest change you notice half the time.

questions.stem: Weber's law states that for a difference to be noticed, two stimuli must differ by:
options: A constant percentage
A constant amount
Exactly 1 ounce
At least 50%
questions.exp: Weber = percentage, not amount.

questions.stem: According to Weber's law, which change is a person LEAST likely to notice?
options: Adding 1 ounce to a 100-ounce weight
Adding 1 ounce to a 10-ounce weight
Adding 10 ounces to a 100-ounce weight
Adding 5 ounces to a 10-ounce weight
questions.exp: 1 ounce is only 1% of 100 ounces, below the 2% needed for weight. The others are 10% or more.

questions.stem: According to Weber's law, about how much must a weight change before a person notices the difference?
options: 1 ounce, no matter the starting weight
10 ounces
questions.exp: Your slides: weight must change by 2%.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why adding 1 ounce is noticeable on a 10-ounce weight but not on a 100-ounce weight?
options: Differences are noticed by percentage, not amount, and 1 ounce is a much bigger percentage of 10 ounces.
Heavier weights raise the absolute threshold for touch.
People use top-down processing only with light weights.
The Stroop effect slows reactions to heavy objects.
questions.exp: Weber's law: a constant percentage, not a constant amount.

questions.stem: A woman claims she can send her thoughts directly into her twin's mind. This claim is called:
options: Telepathy
Clairvoyance
Precognition
Selective attention
questions.exp: Telepathy = mind-to-mind communication.

questions.stem: A man claims he dreamed about a car crash the night before it happened. This claim is called:
options: Precognition
Telepathy
Clairvoyance
The pop-out phenomenon
questions.exp: Precognition = perceiving future events.

questions.stem: Which statement about extrasensory perception (ESP) is most accurate?
options: There is no scientific basis for it, and psychic visions given to police are no more accurate than other people's guesses.
Studies show clairvoyance helps police solve most cases.
Telepathy has been proven in laboratory experiments.
Precognition is a type of bottom-up processing.
questions.exp: Your slides: no scientific basis, and psychics do no better than guesses.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why some people believe psychics are accurate?
options: Psychics make so many predictions that some are bound to be right, and people remember the hits and forget the misses.
Psychics have lower absolute thresholds than other people.
Psychics use top-down processing and other people don't.
Most psychic predictions turn out to be correct.
questions.exp: So many predictions → a few hits; people focus on the 1 or 2 correct ones.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Clairvoyance — perceiving events you didn't witness
Telepathy — perceiving future events
Precognition — mind-to-mind communication
Pop-out phenomenon — failing to notice a change
questions.exp: Telepathy = mind to mind, precognition = the future, and failing to notice a change is change blindness.

sections.name: Mock exam
examTips: Turn the Timer on and answer every question without looking anything up.
Aim for about one minute per question. Flag hard ones and come back.
